**Project Summary (ColliForce-VLA)**

Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are increasingly deployed for robotic manipulation, yet their safety evaluation is fundamentally flawed. Through a large-scale empirical study (70+ experiments, 6,000+ episodes) on SafeLIBERO, we reveal that the standard Collision Avoidance Rate (CAR) is systematically contaminated by "fake safety"—episodes where robots appear safe simply because they stop moving, not because they avoid obstacles.

A Pi0 model with SDF auxiliary loss achieves 91.5% CAR, yet 99.6% of safe episodes show obstacle displacement below 0.1mm—frozen robots, not collision-avoiding ones. We propose displacement-filtered CAR (dfCAR) to distinguish genuine avoidance from action collapse. We further demonstrate a capability-safety anti-correlation: stronger models (Pi0.5, TSR=74.7%) collide more because greater task capability produces more motion. Through controlled LoRA-only versus LoRA+SDF experiments across multiple loss scales, we show explicit SDF geometric supervision contributes zero additional collision avoidance—the signal emerges entirely from implicit patterns in demonstration data. Oracle experiments confirm end-effector-only SDF suffers structural limitations, as arm-body collisions dominate.

Mechanistic analysis reveals that fine-tuning collapse (TSR: 74.7%→6.8%) stems from distribution shift in safety-focused data, not SDF loss itself—LoRA baselines without SDF exhibit identical degradation. The model learns conservative behavior rather than safe behavior.

These findings challenge reported safety metrics across the VLA literature and provide actionable insights: the problem lies in evaluation methodology, not geometric supervision. Our work contributes a corrected evaluation framework and diagnostic evidence redirecting future VLA safety research.

**Paper Abstract (for submission, 240 words)**

Collision Avoidance Rate (CAR) is the de facto safety metric for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models in robotic manipulation. We demonstrate that CAR is systematically contaminated by what we term "fake safety"—episodes classified as collision-free not because the robot actively avoids obstacles, but because it fails to move entirely. Through a large-scale empirical study spanning 70+ experiments and 6,000+ episodes on the SafeLIBERO benchmark, we reveal that a Pi0 model fine-tuned with Signed Distance Function (SDF) auxiliary loss achieves 91.5% CAR while 99.6% of its safe episodes exhibit obstacle displacement below 0.1mm, indicating complete action collapse rather than collision avoidance. We propose displacement-filtered CAR (dfCAR), a corrected metric that filters out episodes lacking meaningful end-effector motion, and demonstrate its robustness across displacement thresholds spanning two orders of magnitude. Our analysis further reveals a capability-safety anti-correlation: stronger base models complete more tasks but collide more frequently, as increased task capability produces greater motion and thus more collision opportunities. Through controlled attribution experiments comparing LoRA-only fine-tuning against LoRA+SDF across multiple loss scales, we find that explicit geometric supervision via SDF contributes zero additional collision avoidance—the avoidance signal emerges entirely from implicit patterns in collision-free demonstration data. Oracle experiments with ground-truth SDF confirm that end-effector-only geometric supervision suffers structural limitations, with arm-body collisions accounting for the majority of contact events. These findings expose a systematic flaw in VLA safety evaluation and redirect future safety method design from geometric supervision toward evaluation methodology reform.
